newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to transport nuclear fuel by air again.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to transport nuclear fuel by air again.

text.p: Bulgaria, anticipating serious difficulties with energy supplies this winter, will transport more nuclear fuel by air from Russia for its Soviet-made Kozloduy power plant, energy officials said on Thursday.
They said they planned to start transporting the fuel for recharging the Kozloduy VVER-1,000 reactor number six by the beginning of October at the latest.
"We will transport the fuel by air until we have completed all the arrangements for the fuel's future land transportation," a senior energy official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
"We are in the process of negotiating consignments of nuclear fuel by land from Russia with Ukraine, Moldova and Romania as we need their agreement," he added.
This autumn's delivery will be the second transportation of nuclear fuel by air for recharging Kozloduy's reactors.
Since the break-up of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria has needed the consent of Ukraine and Moldova to transit its fuel supplies across their territory.
Romania has also insisted on approving Bulgaria's transportation of nuclear fuel on the river Danube.
Last year Romanian Danube shipping authorities detained a barge carrying 106 tonnes of fresh fuel from Ukraine to Kozloduy.
Fresh fuel for recharging the Kozloduy VVER-440 reactors from Russia was received by air for the first time on June 18 and 20.

The National Electricity Company (NEC), which is one of 70 debt-ridden firms barred by the government from drawing bank credits, has arranged with Moscow to pay for its nuclear fuel in portions of some $5-6 million per month.
The State Fund for Reconstruction and Development will guarantee Moscow the NEC's payments for the nuclear fuel worth some $30 million, officials said.
Bulgaria, which imports 80 percent of its energy resources, relies on its Kozloduy four 440-megawatt reactors and two 1,000-megawatt reactors for more than half its energy.
In May, under pressure from the European Union, Bulgaria switched off its controversial and oldest reactor number one for safety tests of the metal of the reactor's vessel.
The taking of samples has been delayed as Westinghouse Electric Corp has not yet finished its preliminary tests, Kozloduy engineers said.
Bulgaria hopes to receive the results of the tests by year-end and to restart the reactor in January if they show the metal is safe.
